items.title: Ergonomics, Robotics, and Disciplinary Integration
items.abstract: Ergonomics is inherently based on disciplinary integration: a compulsory condition to lead the systemic understanding and improvement of real-world complexities like the ones of Human-Robot Interactions (HRIs). Accordingly, this chapter ponders the contributions of diverse disciplines to the study of human factors alongside their synergies with the multi-faceted area of robotics. Key examples are presented, considering problems requiring approaches like bio-inspired soft robotics, value-sensitive design, interactions and affective features, and neuroergonomics in HRI. The implications about education on HRI ergonomics are also pondered. Overall, this chapter remarks how diverse backgrounds can lead to contributions to the human-centered design and assessment of robots if the experts, regardless of disciplinary boundaries, just focus on learning novel perspectives and methods to solve the problems occurring in Human-Robot Systems.

items.title: Ergonomics, Values and Robot Ethics
items.abstract: The development, implementation and use of technological artifacts introduces ethical issues—technologies are not ethically neutral. This ethical dimension is particularly obvious in robotic technologies, as many types and applications of robots are situated at the intersection of automation and social interaction. Consequently, developers, researchers and users of robots are confronted with ethical issues, for example concerning safety or (human) autonomy. With respect to ergonomics, two main themes can be identified: (1) Ergonomics itself involves certain values such as well-being, accessibility, performance optimization, safety, and trust. These values (and others) can and should be discussed in ethical terms. (2) Complex ethical issues in human–robot interaction are often difficult to address and can be cognitively overwhelming in the design process. One common ad-hoc strategy is to simply bypass and ignore these potential issues. However, professional tools that deal with ethical issues in the development and use of robotic system are available and may help to advance values in robotics. The most widely acknowledged framework to address values embedded in socio-technical systems during the development process is Value Sensitive Design (VSD). Focusing on ethical values, we present this framework with respect to robotic technologies. Finally, as implied by the very idea of human–robot interaction, robots themselves can be interpreted as subjects of action. This interpretation suggests an ethical reflection of the actions and behaviors performed by robots as if they were moral agents, an idea that is at odds with the key themes of ergonomics, values and ethics of robotics.

items.title: Ethical Appraisals of Artificial Intelligence in MBA Education: Moral Concern, Social Pressure, Perceived Benefits, and AI Experience
items.abstract: This cross-sectional study examined how MBA students appraise ethical concerns, practical benefits, social expectations, control, and institutional governance related to educational artificial intelligence (AI). The analysis used 275 eligible responses submitted by the prespecified study cut-off. Descriptive statistics, omega and Spearman-Brown reliability, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), rank-based and bootstrap robustness checks, and regression models of ordered AI experience were used. Three exploratory dimensions were retained in 90.4% of 500 bootstrap samples. A proportional-odds reference model improved on the null model, chi-square(6) = 17.81, p = .007, but the proportional-odds assumption was rejected, chi-square(6) = 17.81, p = .007; threshold-specific models were therefore primary. AI self-efficacy/control was associated with reporting at least moderate rather than none/minimal AI experience (OR = 1.51, 95% CI [1.13, 2.03], p = .005), and this result persisted after background adjustment, bootstrap validation, and response-quality screens. In the smaller extensive-experience comparison (n = 26), efficiency benefit and perceived ethical-issue frequency were positive exploratory correlates. Concern was highest for data privacy, while governance responses indicated comparatively limited knowledge of personal-data practices. Predictive performance was modest. The findings support clearer task-specific guidance, critical AI literacy, and transparent data practices, but the cross-sectional self-report design does not establish causal adoption effects or validated moral profiles.

items.title: Evaluating a Large Language Model for Emergency Triage Using Synthetic Clinical Dialogues: Toward a Multimodal Clinical Safety Framework
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Prioritizing patient safety through accurate emergency triage is critical during mass-gathering events such as Hajj and Umrah, where high patient volumes can significantly increase the risk of clinical errors. Although the Emergency Severity Index (ESI) provides a standardized triage protocol, it remains dependent on human judgment, while traditional artificial intelligence (AI) models often struggle to capture the nuanced clinical context embedded in patient narratives. To address this gap, this study evaluates GPT-5.2 using synthetically generated dialogues as a step toward a conceptual clinical decision-support framework that bridges structured electronic health records (EHRs) with triage interactions through clinical dialogues. By combining narrative inputs with structured physiological indicators, it explores the potential to support more informed clinical decision-making under controlled simulation conditions. Methods: To evaluate this contribution, we systematically assessed the role of clinical dialogues in triage performance using a balanced and stratified dataset of 1000 simulated Hajj-context scenarios. Results: The results demonstrate that incorporating clinical dialogues can significantly improve triage performance, with a 79.7% relative reduction in under-triage across all ESI levels. A more noticeable improvement was observed in high-acuity cases, with a 91.9% relative reduction in under-triage. In addition, the model achieved a high-acuity recall of 94.5%, highlighting its ability to identify critical “red-flag” symptoms that are often not captured in structured data. These findings suggest that narrative context may contribute to more accurate triage assessment and improved identification of high-acuity cases. Conclusions: Consequently, when evaluated within a controlled decision-support setting, this study suggests that large language model (LLM)-based systems may improve triage reliability and may contribute to safer triage decision-making in high-demand clinical environments.

items.title: Evidence Is the Key, Not the Log: Cryptographic Execution Control for AI Agents and Autonomous Systems
items.abstract: What if an AI agent could not complete a consequential action until the real-world result of an earlier, bounded action had been independently verified—and that verification was required to unlock the next execution step? As frontier AI models and autonomous agents increasingly operate financial systems, cloud infrastructure, sensitive communications, autonomous machinery, and critical infrastructure, conventional security mechanisms face a fundamental limitation: authorization establishes what is permitted, but does not necessarily establish what actually happened along the real execution path. Audit logs may record a mistake after its consequences become irreversible. Simulations may succeed while the real destination, network route, transaction system, or physical actuator behaves differently. Even a successful initial authorization does not justify unlimited authority to execute subsequent actions. This paper develops a different architectural principle: “Evidence is the key, not the log.” Building on the distinction that computation is not authority to act, the proposed architecture makes independently validated evidence of a preceding real effect a technical prerequisite for later effectuation. The mechanism is called Receipt-Gated Staged Effectuation, supported by an Interim Effectuation Validator (IEV). For selected consequential operations, the architecture authorizes a deliberately bounded but real first effect, rather than immediately releasing the complete consequence. A protected observer, destination, transaction system, network element, storage component, or hardware controller generates an Effect Confirmation Receipt (ECR) describing what actually occurred. The IEV independently verifies the receipt against the authorized Candidate Act, expected effect, phase, destination, sink identity, freshness, policy, revocation state, and authorized scope. Only after successful validation does the protected domain establish the Continuation Authority Object (CAO) required for the next phase. The critical distinction is that the next effect can be made technically impossible—not merely prohibited by policy—until validated evidence from the preceding real effect becomes available. Possible implementations include receipt-derived cryptographic keys, split-key reconstruction, protected internal state, hardware latches, pre-staged non-executable commands, and pre-delivered ciphertext whose final decryption material remains withheld. Unlike ordinary canary deployment or post-execution monitoring, the earlier phase's evidence becomes part of the causal authority chain. Its receipt is not merely information about the previous operation; it is a required input to the authority enabling the next operation. The paper develops: Three effectuation modes: Direct protected single-phase execution, bounded demonstration followed by full effectuation, and progressive multi-phase execution. Adaptive effectuation: Geometric and risk-dependent progression, reversibility-aware phase sizing, nested stages, and parallel effectuation. Cryptographic causal dependency: Receipt-derived execution material, split credentials, tokenless continuation, hardware-gated enablement, and protected state transitions. Protected evidence semantics: Proof of delivery versus proof of effect, negative receipts, receipt freshness, destination binding, cross-device protection, Merkle receipt structures, and privacy-preserving confirmation. Independent continuation authority: Human, automatic, hybrid, and multi-authority decisions separated from the potentially compromised AI-agent environment. Fail-closed recovery: Missing or conflicting receipts, uncertain outcomes, replay protection, atomic consumption, reconciliation, and prevention of blind retries. Anti-bypass enforcement: Protected execution boundaries, credential surrogation, taint and provenance controls, alternative-path closure, and software–hardware implementation independence. A principal contribution is a catalogue of 146 numbered technical embodiments, organized into 19 groups, covering AI-agent tool execution, messages and file delivery, payments and settlement, data export, cloud and model deployment, databases, persistent model memory, GPUs and accelerators, robotics, industrial controllers, vehicles, UAVs, telecommunications, satellite systems, and distributed infrastructure. Illustrative workflows show how sensitive communications may release a limited verification object before the full payload; how a bounded payment authorization may precede settlement; how verified cloud canary results may gate broader deployment; and how measured physical movement may enable subsequent actuator authority. In each staged example, the initial effect is real—not merely simulated—and subsequent authority depends on protected validation of its observed result. The central research proposition is that evidence should not merely explain what happened after execution. For selected high-consequence operations, independently verified evidence should determine whether further execution is technically possible. The architecture does not require every operation to be staged. Protected policy may authorize single-phase execution where the consequence model permits it. Nor does validation of one phase guarantee that all later outcomes will be correct. The design instead establishes bounded, conditional progression under explicit trust and enforcement assumptions. This publication provides a technical architecture, formal relationships, execution workflows, and a catalogue of embodiments. It is a design and analytical contribution, not an experimentally validated implementation. Patent pending: The document identifies the related invention as “Systems and Methods for Cryptographically Staged Effectuation with Verified Partial Effect, Receipt-Bound Full Effectuation, and Software-Hardware Enforcement.” No conclusion concerning patentability, enforceable patent scope, infringement, or implementation by any particular commercial system is asserted. Invitation for independent technical validation: Frontier AI providers, security architects, researchers, hardware engineers, distributed-systems specialists, and critical-infrastructure operators are invited to examine the 146 embodiments, identify relevant prior art, evaluate the receipt-to-authority dependency, challenge the anti-bypass assumptions, and propose alternative implementations. Independent criticism, adversarial testing, and evidence-based technical conclusions are welcomed.

items.title: Evolution of Capability Leadership: From Leading People to Enabling Organisational Capability in the AI Era
items.abstract: Evolution of Capability Leadership opens the seven-part Capability Leadership Series by examining how leadership enables people, collective judgement, work systems and technology to deliver reliable, responsible and sustained organisational outcomes.Drawing on NASA’s documented approach to capability leadership, the paper develops a broader interpretation for the AI era. It proposes a definition of Capability Leadership and examines the conditions through which expertise can be applied, decisions acted upon and capability sustained as work changes.The discussion connects leadership responsibility with human judgement, human–AI collaboration, workplace learning and TechnoEthics. Practical workplace examples help leaders consider how authority, access to expertise, coordination, oversight and opportunities for learning affect the outcomes their organisations depend on.CLS-01 establishes the conceptual foundation for the series and invites leaders and practitioners to examine what must change for organisational capability to be developed, applied, trusted and sustained.

items.title: Examining the effect of work-life integration on burnout among Indonesian employees
items.abstract: Background: Burnout remains a critical occupational health issue in Indonesia. While previous studies often focus on static Work-Life Balance, modern workplace requires a dynamic Work-Life Integration (WLI) approach, yet dimensions mitigating burnout remain unclear.Purpose: This study investigates how WLI affects employee burnout and identifies specific dimensions acting as protective factors or stressors, alongside demographic boundary conditions.Method: A cross-sectional survey involved 355 employees (Mage = 32.08, SD = 10; 67.9% male and 32.1% female) across Western, Central, and Eastern Indonesia. Data were collected using the Maslach-Trisni Burnout Inventory (𝛼 = .916) and transadapted Work-Life Indicator Scale with internal consistency for WLI dimensions ranging from 𝛼 = .664 to .837. Regression and correlation analyses were conducted using SPSS and Multigroup Analysis (PLS-MGA) using SmartPLS.Findings: Multidimensional WLI predicts burnout (R2 = 17.6%). Work Identity (b = -.269) and Boundary Control (b = -.131) protect against burnout, whereas Non-Work Interrupting Work acts as a stressor. PLS-MGA reveals that Work Interrupting Non-work intensifies burnout specifically among permanent and single employees.Discussion: Professional identity and boundary management appear more critical than role fusion in preventing burnout, highlighting the need for targeted, demographic-sensitive boundary management addressing vulnerabilities related to employment status and marital demands.

items.abstract: La incorporación de tecnologías digitales en la educación superior no garantiza por sí sola transformaciones pedagógicas significativas si no está acompañada de una reflexión didáctica crítica sobre sus finalidades y modos de uso. En este marco, esta investigación analiza la incorporación de materiales didácticos interactivos autoadministrados, diseñados con apoyo de inteligencia artificial (IA), según el modelo de sustitución, aumento, modificación y redefinición (SAMR) y en clave problematizadora, en comparación con clases presenciales tradicionales, en el curso introductorio de la Facultad de Información y Comunicación (FIC) de la Universidad de la República (Udelar) de Uruguay. Este curso es obligatorio para todo el estudiantado de ingreso, tiene como propósito ofrecer información sobre la oferta formativa de la FIC, su estructura académica, instalaciones y espacios de referencia institucionales. La intervención, dirigida a 1254 estudiantes inscritos de las licenciaturas en Comunicación, Archivología y Bibliotecología, consistió en sustituir las presentaciones presenciales iniciales de las unidades curriculares del primer semestre por un módulo virtual interactivo que integró múltiples lenguajes, navegación condicionada, un espacio colaborativo asíncrono y una encuesta de retroalimentación. El diseño promovió un recorrido autónomo y progresivo del contenido, habilitando la reflexión individual y colectiva. Se recogieron 831 respuestas a la encuesta (66.3 %) y 628 publicaciones en el espacio colaborativo (50.1 %). Esto permitió evaluar percepciones, niveles de apropiación conceptual y evidencias de autorregulación. This mandatory course is aimed at all first-year students and seeks to provide information about the FIC’s academic offerings, academic structure, facilities, and institutional reference spaces. This module incorporated multiple media, conditional navigation, an asynchronous collaborative space, and a feedback survey. The design encouraged a self-guided and progressive exploration of content, enabling both individual and collective reflection. A total of 831 responses to the survey (66.3%) and 628 posts in the collaborative space (50.1%) were collected, allowing for the evaluation of perceptions, conceptual appropriation levels, and evidence of self-regulated learning. items.title: Exploring learning in classic African board games: a review of recent literature
items.abstract: Abstract A growing body of research on board games demonstrates that these games can function as learning environments and provide opportunities for learning across diverse contexts. Although learning is often conceptualized contextually within this literature, studies increasingly demonstrate that meaningful learning can occur through participation in board game environments. However, the relationship between board games and learning has been examined predominantly through the study of modern board games, with comparatively limited attention given to classic African board games. This literature review explores learning in classic African board games. This study serves two purposes as it highlights the state of research on classic African board games and the relationship of these games with learning. The fi ndings show that classic African board games are spaces where learning occurs and players engage in a constellation of literacies. The studies analyzed indicate that playing these games can facilitate mathematical learning, engage players in computational thinking and songoputation, and foster the development of skills related to science, engineering, and technology (i.e. STEM). These board games also allow for the exploration of artificial intelligence (AI), which results in the learning of new AI techniques. Classic African board games have the potential to simplify the learning of various subjects and the acquisition of skills relevant to the 21st century. As such, more empirical studies should be conducted to further investigate the connection between playing thesegames, their game mechanics and learning; and particularly the link between their gameplay and the learning of specific subjects such as mathematics, science, and engineering.

items.title: Exploring The Role of AI and Educational Factors in Shaping Academic Performance in Accounting Education in South African Universities: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming teaching and learning in accounting education. While AI technologies offer opportunities to enhance learning outcomes, academic performance is also influenced by broader educational factors such as teacher competence, institutional support, curriculum design, and student engagement. This study investigates the role of AI and educational factors in shaping academic performance in accounting education through a systematic literature review of studies published between 2020 and 2025. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a structured search of major academic databases yielded 168 initial records. After screening and eligibility assessment, 28 studies were retained for final analysis. The review synthesizes empirical evidence on AI applications in accounting education and identifies key factors influencing student performance. The study is grounded in Human Capital Theory and Social Cognitive Theory, which provide insights into how technological and educational investments influence learning outcomes. The findings reveal that AI technologies such as intelligent tutoring systems, generative AI tools, predictive analytics, and automated assessment platforms enhance academic performance through personalized learning and data-driven feedback. However, the effectiveness of these technologies depends on teacher digital competence, student motivation, curriculum alignment, and institutional support. The study proposes an integrated conceptual framework linking AI adoption and educational factors to academic performance in accounting education. The findings provide implications for educators, policymakers, and curriculum developers seeking to improve accounting education in the digital era.

items.title: From Human Judgment to Machine Learning: A Philosophical Study of Knowledge Creation in Modern Accounting
items.abstract: Background: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning into accounting and auditing has transformed the creation, validation, and application of professional knowledge, raising questions about the legitimacy of algorithmic knowledge in accounting practice. Objective: This study examines the epistemological shift from human judgment to algorithmic knowledge in the implementation of Financial Accounting Standards (Standar Akuntansi Keuangan [SAK]) and Quality Management Systems (Sistem Manajemen Mutu [SMM]). Methods: This study employs a qualitative-interpretive approach through conceptual analysis and an examination of practitioners’ perspectives on the reliability, transparency, explainability, and trustworthiness of AI-assisted decision-making. Results: The results of the study show that AI can improve efficiency, predictive accuracy, and analytical capabilities in modern accounting practices but, at the same time, poses epistemological challenges in the form of limited algorithmic transparency, limited explainability, and the potential erosion of auditors’ professional skepticism. Although the conceptual analysis indicates that AI can positively affect efficiency and predictive accuracy, it also raises epistemic challenges related to transparency, accountability, and the preservation of professional skepticism. The shift from judgment-based knowledge to data-driven inferential knowledge has transformed the traditional epistemic authority held by accountants and auditors. The application of SAK and SMM in the accounting profession has implications for defining professional responsibilities in maintaining the quality of financial reporting and audit processes. Conclusion: This study proposes a human–machine epistemic partnership, in which AI functions as an analytical augmentation tool while accountants and auditors remain the primary epistemic authorities.

items.title: From image biomarkers to treatment decisions: multimodal AI and clinical translation in gynecologic oncology
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly expanding across gynecologic oncology, but most applications remain focused on image interpretation and retrospective prediction rather than direct support of treatment decisions. This review examines how AI is progressing from imaging biomarkers toward multimodal decision-support systems that integrate radiologic, pathologic, molecular, and clinical information. We summarize current applications in ovarian, endometrial, and cervical cancers, with particular attention to preoperative risk stratification, surgical planning, radiotherapy, systemic treatment selection, treatment-response prediction, and multidisciplinary decision-making. Multimodal approaches are especially promising because they reflect the way clinical decisions are made and may provide greater value than models based on a single data source. However, the current evidence remains dominated by retrospective and often single-center studies, with limited external and prospective validation. Data heterogeneity, domain shift, incomplete multimodal datasets, bias, workflow integration, regulatory requirements, and model monitoring remain important barriers to routine implementation. We therefore outline a stepwise pathway for clinical translation, from robust multicenter validation and prospective human–AI evaluation to clinical-impact studies and post-deployment monitoring. The next phase of AI in gynecologic oncology should prioritize clinically meaningful decisions and measurable patient or workflow benefit rather than incremental gains in predictive performance alone.

items.title: From Individual Chatbot Interaction to the Virtual Tutor with Physical Presence: Comparing Educational Interaction Models with Conversational AI
items.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence can provide individual study support, but the educational significance of its responses depends on how they are examined and used. We develop a conceptual framework comparing Individual Chatbot Interaction and Standard Classroom Interaction, then specify a Virtual Tutor with Physical Presence as a situated implementation of shared AI inquiry. The framework draws on selected scholarship concerning mediated learning, educational dialogue, self-regulation, cognitive engagement, pedagogical agents, and AI literacy. We define the unit of analysis as an interaction episode and distinguish private consultation, shared instruction, and hybrid activities through observable criteria. The tutor is specified as an animated avatar projected by video-mapping onto a static volumetric surface in the classroom; perceived presence and learning are treated as outcomes requiring measurement. The proposed contribution is a design specification linking public AI responses, teacher orchestration, evidence-based scrutiny, and individual reflection. An explanatory pathway connects these conditions to possible cognitive and metacognitive processes, with four propositions and matched comparisons for future evaluation. A projected avatar is neither necessary nor sufficient for collective verification, and its incremental value must be tested against simpler shared interfaces. No empirical effectiveness is claimed. The framework provides a basis for investigating when a situated conversational tutor supports disciplinary understanding and critical AI use.

items.title: From Instructional Intent to Classroom-Ready Lessons: Investigating Teacher-AI Collaboration in Lesson Authoring for Secondary Computing Education
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly studied as a tool for supporting lesson authoring; the creation and adaptation of classroom materials, yet little is known about how it should fit into secondary computing teachers' subject-specific practices. We conducted two complementary qualitative studies with eight secondary computing teachers: focus groups examining existing authoring practices and a think-aloud study using LessonBuilder, a structured AI-supported lesson authoring system, as a research probe. We found that teachers' instructional intentions developed through creating, inspecting, and adapting materials, while teachers selectively delegated tasks to AI and retained responsibility for judging classroom readiness. The think-aloud sessions further showed how examining AI-generated materials prompted teachers to clarify and refine their intentions, making authoring an ongoing negotiation between what teachers intended and what the AI produced. In the context of computing lessons, classroom readiness also involved considering how programming materials and supporting guidance matched students' understanding and intended learning goals. We synthesize these findings into a conceptual model explaining how teachers coordinate instructional intent, AI assistance, and judgments of classroom readiness during lesson authoring. We derive design recommendations for supporting this coordination while preserving teacher control and addressing computing-specific authoring needs.

items.title: From medical to pedagogical care
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) agents, including chatbots and virtual tutors, into education has expanded rapidly; however, systematic quantitative analysis of research trends in this field remains limited. Notably, the intellectual foundations of AI agent research lie not in education but in medicine, where AI agents were first extensively deployed and studied in clinical, experimental, and pedagogical contexts. METHODS: In this study, a bibliometric analysis of 377 records retrieved from the Web of Science was conducted using VOSviewer to map the evolution, thematic focus, and collaborative networks within this field. RESULTS: The study showed AI agent research originated strongly in healthcare, with educational applications emerging more recently. Key research themes encompassed AI technologies, human-computer interaction, pedagogical applications, and ethical considerations. Collaborative efforts were led by the USA and China, supported by active European and Asian research hubs. The findings revealed a dual narrative of significant benefits for personalized learning and learner well-being alongside persistent challenges such as algorithmic bias and accessibility gaps. CONCLUSION: To realize the transformative potential of AI in education, future research should prioritize the development of adaptive algorithms, robust ethical frameworks, inclusive design, and interdisciplinary collaboration. By focusing on these areas, the field can work toward overcoming technical, ethical, and logistical barriers, thereby ensuring that AI acts as a sustainable force for equity and excellence in education.

items.title: From Observation to Intervention: Identifiability of Latent User Bias in Human-AI Interaction
items.abstract: Alignment methods typically treat user behavior as a reliable proxy for underlying preferences. However, this assumption breaks down when users hold belief-dependent cognitive biases, risking irreversible ``confirmation traps'' and harmful feedback loops. In this paper, we formalize when an AI system can distinguish true user preferences from behavior shaped by cognitive bias. Modeling this interaction as a multi-armed bandit, we first prove a non-identifiability theorem: under passive observation, a static binary biased user produces action trajectory distributions strictly identical to an unbiased user in a transformed environment, forcing any action-only estimator to perform no better than random guessing. We then show that active preference elicitation breaks this observational equivalence. Specifically, we prove that an Observer applying a finite sequence of adversarial zero-reward interventions of length $m_δ$ makes the post-intervention action distributions arbitrarily separable. Our theoretical results suggest that robust alignment requires actively intervening to tell informed preferences from biases.

items.title: From Theory to Trends: A Bibliometric Review of Job Crafting and Subjective Well-Being in the Context of Sustainable Work
items.abstract: The literature review of the paper on job crafting and subjective well-being relies on bibliometric analysis. The key conclusions are that such categories like Commerce, Management, Human Resources and Industry, Tourism and Services, and Human Society and Psychology prevail. There are evident conceptual clusters, e.g. work engagement and job resources-demands and emerging themes such as well-being in digital and educational environment. The review shows the fast field development and identifies the future research directions that would include digital work settings, cross-cultural research, and long-term research. The existing knowledge can assist the researchers and practitioners in enhancing the employee welfare and attaining sustainable organizational performance. Although there is literature on narrative and empirical research, there has been a dearth of systematic mapping, yet this review identifies the growth of job crafting and well-being research into fields of education, health sciences and information systems. The future research directions are multi-region studies, the significance of digital transformation, and sustainable work design. On the whole, it is possible to note that the given review presents the current knowledge and focuses on digital work environments, cross-cultural viewpoints, and longitudinal approaches to the issue. Its results are relevant to management practice in addressing the contemporary workplace issues.

items.title: Fusion of Flexible Sensors and Computer Vision for Biomechanical Modeling of Simulated Wind Turbine Maintenance Operations
items.abstract: Accurate biomechanical modeling is essential for assessing musculoskeletal loading during occupational tasks, but traditional laboratory motion capture is often impractical for field applications. This study developed and evaluated a sensor fusion framework combining flexible wearable sensors with single-view mobile video keypoints for biomechanical modeling of simulated wind turbine maintenance operations. Eighteen healthy participants performed three tasks: symmetric lifting, bolt-torque tensioning, and ladder climbing. Motion was captured simultaneously using 13 BioStamp flexible sensors, a marker-based motion capture system, and mobile video processed with pose detection algorithms. A convolutional neural network was trained using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation to predict whole-body joint angles referenced to OpenSim inverse kinematics. The fusion model achieved an average RMSE of 9.3°, improving estimation accuracy by 5% compared with the sensor-only model and 21% compared with the video-only model. Findings suggest that combining flexible sensors with video-derived keypoints offers a scalable approach for field-based occupational biomechanics assessment.

items.title: Future of Anticipatory Robotics in Manufacturing
items.abstract: Collaborative robots, designed to work alongside humans in shared environments, are transforming manufacturing production lines, enabling partial automation and boosting productivity. But their potential extends beyond these benefits. By implementing anticipatory strategies to prevent workers’ risky behaviours and reduce excessive workloads, collaborative robots can proactively enhance working conditions. For example, they can take on repetitive or strenuous tasks to reduce physical effort or adjust the pace of operations to help alleviate stress levels. Indeed, Musculoskeletal Disorders (MSDs) and Common Mental Disorders (CMDs), which arise from uncontrolled physical and cognitive loads, are major work-related health problems in developed countries, with incommensurate social and economic costs. Collaborative robots can curb the effect of such disorders and help in preserving workers’ health. This Chapter addresses how Human Factors and Ergonomics (HFE) can be monitored to provide robots with relevant inputs about the human state, and how robots can be employed to improve HFE. Novel strategies are proposed to adapt online robot behaviour to the workers’ psycho-physical state and enhance their well-being and productivity.

items.title: GAI hallucinations and user dependence: cognitive-affective responses and individual differences
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) hallucinations raise questions about how users respond to unreliable outputs from a technology on which they depend. Drawing on the cognitive–affective components of the Interaction of Person–Affect–Cognition–Execution (I-PACE) framework, this study examines the roles of GAI trust, cognitive dissonance, perceived controllability, and frustration in the relationship between perceived hallucinations and GAI dependence, with GAI literacy and self-efficacy as individual-difference moderators. A between-subjects experiment involved 546 participants who viewed the same GAI dialogue labelled as either containing fabricated information or verified as accurate. Participants in the former condition reported lower trust and perceived controllability, greater cognitive dissonance and frustration, and lower dependence scores. In the parallel model, the indirect associations through trust, controllability, and frustration were negative, whereas the indirect association through cognitive dissonance was positive. Higher GAI literacy weakened the positive controllability–dependence association. The remaining moderation hypotheses were not supported under the directional and multiplicity-adjusted criteria. The findings connect users’ evaluations of unreliable GAI responses with the difficulties they report in regulating their use. They underscore the importance of examining dependence alongside reliability judgements, cognitive conflict, and emotional reactions when assessing the human consequences of GAI hallucinations.

items.title: Generative AI and technological mediation: writing micro-processes, products and perceptions
items.abstract: The public release of ChatGPT presents language education with both advantages and challenges. Being widely available and readily producing texts at user's command, it is an especially useful resource in ESL writing. However, to be able to leverage it effectively for that purpose, we need to understand the writing micro-processes surrounding its use. To this end, this study investigates, through an experimental design, writing micro-processes along with writing outcomes, and perceptions of 12 ESL writers across three writing conditions. The data included interviews, questionnaires as well as essay grades and screen recordings. Two of the three conditions involved the use of ChatGPT. The results indicate that the majority of participants favored the ChatGPT- assisted conditions and noted its role in aiding idea generation. Despite this preference, some participants noted that ChatGPT-produced texts felt robotic and lacked a human touch. We found no statistically significant differences across the three conditions in the participants' essays. Most notably, our analysis identified distinct clusters of writing micro-processes associated with the ChatGPT conditions, suggesting that generative AI tools can influence writing behaviors although the link to outcomes is not straightforward. These findings provide insights into the potential benefits and limitations of using AI tools in writing tasks. The article discusses areas for further research to enhance the integration of AI into ESL writing education.

items.title: Generative AI in Entrepreneurship: Applications, Opportunities, Challenges and Future Directions
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming entrepreneurship by helping entrepreneurs generate ideas, analyze information, create content, develop business models, support marketing, and make decisions. This review examines the growing role of GenAI in entrepreneurial activities, with a focus on opportunity recognition, creativity, innovation, SMEs, emerging economies, and responsible AI use. GenAI can reduce resource constraints and provide affordable support to small businesses, but challenges such as inaccurate information, overdependence, privacy concerns, and unequal digital skills remain. The article highlights the importance of human–AI collaboration and introduces the concept of AI entrepreneurial capability, which includes AI literacy, effective prompting, evaluation of AI outputs, decision-making, and responsible use of AI. The review concludes that future entrepreneurship should focus not only on using AI to generate more opportunities but also on improving the quality, sustainability, and responsible development of those opportunities.

items.title: Governing Academic Integrity in AI-Enabled Higher Education Ecosystems: A Systematic-Narrative Review of Assessment Technology, Risk and Strategy
items.abstract: AI-enabled assessment technologies are increasingly used by higher education institutions to protect academic integrity, scale online assessment and respond strategically to generative artificial intelligence. This paper examines how online proctoring, automated scoring, AI writing detection, and learning analytics risk flagging reshape institutional governance, stakeholder trust, and assessment strategy in higher education business ecosystems. Using a systematic-narrative review approach informed by PRISMA 2020 reporting principles, the study synthesises peer-reviewed literature and authoritative policy guidance published between 2015 and 2025. The analysis is organised around an integrated theoretical framework that combines assessment validity, academic integrity values, algorithmic accountability, and ecosystem strategy. The findings show that AI-enabled assessment can support identity verification, monitoring capacity, workflow triage and timely feedback when deployed as human-governed decision support rather than automated adjudication. However, over-reliance on surveillance and detection creates strategic risks: false positives, bias against linguistically diverse students, privacy intrusion, opaque decision-making, weakened due process and construct distortion when assessments measure surveillance compliance instead of intended learning outcomes. The review further shows that institutional legitimacy depends less on the technical promise of tools and more on governance capability, including proportionality, transparency, contestability, equity auditing, privacy protection and authentic assessment redesign. The paper contributes to business ecosystem and strategy scholarship by positioning academic integrity technology as a strategic governance issue within higher education service ecosystems. It recommends integrity-by-design, cross-functional AI governance, vendor accountability and assessment strategies that preserve fairness, validity and stakeholder trust.

items.title: Governing Human-AI Systems: A Co-Agency Equilibrium Model for Dynamic Authority Allocation and Accountability
items.abstract: Human–AI decision authority is analyzed in relation to changes in relative competence and decision risk, taking institutional oversight capacity into account. The proposed Co-Agency Equilibrium Theory (CAET) and Co-Agency Equilibrium Model (CAEM) offer a sociotechnical perspective on humans and AI working as co-agents with varying shares of decision authority. CAET connects the four dimensions, including relative competence, moral salience, irreversibility, and institutional context, with the human authority share and Accountability Gap between delegated risk and human vigilance capability. CAEM combines a logistic policy surface, accountability gap feedback and a gradual adjustment of the human control level, with a switch to full human control if moral salience or irreversibility reaches or exceeds the corresponding threshold. Monotonicity and convergence results are obtained for the model under certain assumptions, and comparative statics illustrate the impact of threshold choices on the escalation region. Simulations in which moral salience and irreversibility are varied separately show the effects of threshold choices on the timing of human takeover under more cautious and more risk-tolerant authority-allocation policies. The framework serves as a blueprint for designing human-AI control logic with normative constraints and deciding on the right level of AI authority based on performance, stakes and domain-specific accountability considerations.

items.title: HFE Considerations in Sustainability in Robotics
items.abstract: Sustainability can be conceptualized as three interlinked aspects: economic; social; and natural capital. In this chapter we will examine what is required for each of these aspects from a human factors and ergonomics perspective to enable sustainability in human-robotic systems. When looking at the economic and social capital nexus it is important to take into account issues of safety and the future roles of humans in robotic systems. This includes issues such as skills, training, resilience, and employment status of the humans. Furthermore, the possibilities arising from advanced social robotics also requires an examination of issues such as privacy, trust, and understandability. When looking at the economic and natural capital nexus it is necessary to consider aspects such as the materials used to produce, maintain, and deconstruct robotic systems as well as the eco-efficiencies and eco-effectiveness that can be obtained from including robotics in human systems. Such an examination requires a consideration of the diverse impact of robotic systems in different geographical communities, and among regions with different economic development status. The social and natural capital nexus requires us to evaluate when and where to invest in human-robotic systems, but also when and where to resist such developments. Finally, we consider the HFE values that are needed to help develop a more sustainable approach to the development of human-robotic systems.

items.title: How media narratives shape public sentiment toward electric micromobility: Stronger effects for e-scooters than e-bikes
items.abstract: Public sentiment toward electric micromobility, particularly e-scooters and e-bikes, is increasingly shaping safety debates and regulatory responses; yet, these attitudes and perceptions have not been systematically evaluated within a unified framework, nor is it clear to what extent they reflect stable judgments versus sensitivity to external narratives. This study addresses these gaps by quantifying public sentiment toward e-bikes and e-scooters and evaluating their responsiveness to controlled negative media narrative exposure. A unified survey framework was developed to enable consistent evaluation, combining statement-based measures with image-based scenario assessments. Two complementary studies were conducted with Australian participants. Study 1 (N = 1027) established baseline sentiment in the absence of media exposure, and Study 2 (N = 1025) examined how responses shift following controlled exposure to negative news headlines. The results showed that public sentiment is multi-dimensional and mixed. While both modes received moderate recognition in terms of sustainability and legitimacy, practical acceptance remained lower, particularly for e-scooters. Exposure to negative media narratives produced broader and more consistent shifts toward less favorable sentiments for e-scooters, especially in perceptions of rider behavior and public-space interaction, whereas e-bike responses remained comparatively stable and more robust to media narrative exposure. In contrast, evaluations of concrete negative situations showed no systematic change following exposure, indicating that these evaluations are grounded in situational interpretation rather than external framing. The findings suggest that public sentiment should be used cautiously to inform policy development. While consistent concerns linked to observable safety issues justify targeted interventions, broader sentiment shifts may reflect narrative influence rather than actual conditions. Effective policy should therefore be informed not only by public sentiment but also by objective evidence on behavior, exposure, and risk.

items.title: How Middle-Power Coordination Can Shape Frontier AI Governance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) middle powers are already shaping international AI governance, from the Bletchley, Seoul, Paris, and India AI Summits to initiatives such as the Hiroshima AI Process and the International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science (formerly the International Network of AI Safety Institutes). Their diplomatic, institutional, regulatory, economic, and technical strengths, however, remain unevenly distributed. “Shared sovereignty,” a strategic pathway identified by Chatham House, offers one way for AI middle powers to pool complementary strengths with like-minded countries and build collective leverage around international AI red lines, particularly limits on unacceptable AI uses and behaviours. This inquiry asks when and how coordination can turn unevenly distributed national capabilities into collective leverage. It examines six middle powers beyond Europe: Brazil, Canada, India, Japan, South Korea, and Singapore, across four episodes of international AI governance. The analysis compares different coordination configurations, the mechanisms and instruments they use, and the conditions under which they generate collective leverage. The findings show that broad participation does not necessarily produce sustained coordination. Middle powers bring complementary strengths, but no single country consistently combines the capabilities needed to influence technical, regulatory, institutional, and diplomatic domains. Coordination generates leverage when these strengths are converted into mechanisms and instruments that produce observable effects. The Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Framework illustrates this dynamic. Developed with support from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) to monitor voluntary adoption of the Hiroshima AI Process International Code of Conduct, the framework translates international commitments into structured reporting on risk management, incident reporting, and information sharing. Its adoption by AI developers created a common reporting structure and generated comparable information on how companies were implementing the Code. This episode suggests that the effects a coordination instrument produces, and the governance arrangements that enable them, can matter as much as its level of institutionalisation when developing mechanisms for behavioural red lines. The analysis identifies five conditions that enable coordination to translate into collective leverage: relational coordination, capability mobilisation, institutional output, governance location, and observable effect. For middle powers, these findings point to five practical priorities: (i) use international and plurilateral forums strategically to identify partners and build support for shared governance objectives; (ii) connect complementary capabilities and authorities across points of interdependence in the AI stack, from model development and evaluation to deployment and risk management, around specific risks and potential red lines; (iii) convert shared commitments into workable assessment, reporting, and response mechanisms; (iv) target governance locations where authority, incentives, and implementation capacity can influence developer behaviour; and (v) assess whether these mechanisms produce observable effects by strengthening shared safety evaluation, monitoring, and technical capacity.

items.title: How trust shapes human reliance on AI decision support in healthcare: A simulation-based behavioral study
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) based decision support systems are increasingly used in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, making it important to understand how trust relates to the use of AI recommendations. Although trust can support effective human–AI collaboration, miscalibrated trust may contribute to inappropriate recommendation acceptance and reduced decision performance. This study examined associations among perceived AI performance, trust, AI recommendation acceptance, and decision accuracy under different levels of AI reliability. In a simulation-based experiment, 100 medical students completed clinical decision-making tasks with AI assistance under high- and low-reliability conditions. Perceived AI performance and trust were measured after each block, while recommendation acceptance and decision accuracy were recorded at the trial level. Mixed-effects models showed that perceived AI performance was positively associated with trust. Higher trust was associated with greater overall acceptance of AI recommendations and greater acceptance of incorrect recommendations. Conversely, higher trust was associated with lower odds of rejecting correct recommendations, indicating more frequent rejection at lower trust. Greater misalignment between normalized trust and objective AI reliability was associated with lower decision accuracy. These findings indicate that calibrated trust is important for effective AI-assisted decision making. They also support the development and evaluation of AI interfaces that communicate reliability and uncertainty to help users align trust with system capability.

items.title: HRI, Culture, and Social Anxiety
items.abstract: Culture and social anxiety are among the human factors influencing the social acceptance of robots. In this chapter, research results are presented based on comparisons among nations conducted by the author’s research group, consisting of those about attitudes toward robots, assumptions about and images of robots, Frankenstein Syndrome, and roboethics. Then, an overview of social anxiety-related research in the field of human–robot interaction (HRI) is provided, regarding on fear of negative evaluation and gaze impact, impact of social anxiety on anxiety and tension during interactions with robots, and effects of social anxiety on robot preference in dialogue situations. Finally, the possibility of interaction effects between cultural factors and social anxiety in HRI is discussed and some future research directions are proposed.

items.title: Human-AI Work Redistribution Across the Software Development Life Cycle: A Socio-Technical Study of Indonesian Developers
items.abstract: AI Coding Assistants are becoming increasingly integrated into software development, changing not only how developers perform their tasks but also how humans and AI share responsibilities. However, how this redistribution of work occurs across the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates how responsibilities are distributed between developers and AI across SDLC activities, how these changes affect software engineering workflows and developer roles, and which socio-technical factors influence this process. Semi-structured interviews with seven software professionals in Indonesia were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The results identify three patterns of human-AI work redistribution: AI-delegated, AI-augmented, and human-controlled work. AI contributes more substantially to structured, repetitive, and relatively verifiable activities, particularly code generation, debugging, testing, and documentation. In contrast, requirements analysis, architectural decisions, security assessment, and release approval remain largely under human control because they require contextual understanding, professional judgment, and accountability. The findings also indicate a shift in developer responsibilities. This redistribution depends on developer experience, AI literacy, trust, model capability, task complexity, security requirements, team practices, and organizational policies. Drawing on socio-technical systems theory and activity theory, the study develops an empirically grounded Human-AI Work Redistribution Model that conceptualizes AI-assisted software engineering as a selective redistribution of responsibilities rather than uniform automation across the SDLC.

items.title: Human–Robot Interaction and Ergonomics
items.abstract: Robots in the workplace are becoming a familiar sight. Hence, they have become the focus of debates and research on workplace ergonomics. While this emerging technology holds great promise to improve environments, this can only be achieved through the intentional application of ergonomic principles. Physical, cognitive and organizational ergonomics must be considered when talking about human-robot interaction (HRI) in a work environment. This chapter presents fundamentals on both human-robot interaction and ergonomics. This includes key topics such as potential roles of humans in HRI, interaction design and interfaces. Furthermore, it presents key domains of HRI and the emerging perspectives in research and application. It underscores the importance of an interdisciplinary approach in assessing the impact of robotics on humans and emphasizes the need for a human-centered design philosophy when developing innovative robotic systems.

items.title: Human–Robot Interaction in Industrial Contexts
items.abstract: Technological advances in industrial robotics have significantly changed modern working environments, enabling greater autonomy, flexibility and productivity. Here the emergence of advanced robots designed for direct interaction with humans play a substantial role. By integrating emerging technologies such as AI, machine learning, and sophisticated interaction design, advanced robots are reshaping industries. All while increasing efficiency and customization and remaining cost-effective. Despite their benefits, the use of robotic systems also brings challenges, particularly in the area of occupational safety and health. After an overview of the evolution of different robotic systems, a description of industrial work tasks, related working conditions and highlighted risk and opportunities associated with automation, this chapter examines key safety factors that are essential for close human–robot interaction and assesses their impact on workers. Two case studies illustrate how the practical application of advanced robotic systems in industrial settings affects workplace dynamics. The chapter further highlights the role of worker expectations and experience in relation to advanced robotics. By combining empirical evidence with real-world applications, this chapter underscores the importance of adaptable, user-friendly robotic systems that prioritize worker well-being alongside operational efficiency. In doing so, it contributes to the broader dialogue on sustainable, ergonomic innovation in the workplace and highlights the critical role of human-centered design in the future of industrial robotics.

items.title: Humanize MLE Agents: Multi-Agent Session Alternation Beyond Single-Agent Limits
items.abstract: Existing LLM-based agent approaches for long-horizon machine learning engineering (MLE) often use context engineering, implemented through custom harnesses that manage tools, skills, and accumulated experience. However, we find that as single-session execution lengthens, the agent's reasoning intensity declines alongside slowing progress, summarized as long-horizon deceleration, and the benefits of these custom harnesses vanish as the underlying model improves, summarized as harness staleness. These findings suggest that their benefits may not persist across versions, which motivates a workflow-level approach in which agents build on one another's work across sessions. We model these alternating agent sessions as a context-reset semi-Markov decision process (CR-SMDP) and establish sufficient conditions for alternation to exceed single-agent reference limits, derive an explicit experiment-budget bound, and characterize when session caps preserve this advantage. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Humanize MLE Agents (HMA), which alternates two agents on a shared workspace, limits each session to at most k experiments and resets the context between sessions, without additional task-specific harness or prior knowledge supplements. Across 75 Kaggle tasks in MLE-bench, HMA reaches a state-of-the-art any-medal rate of 78.2%, exceeding the strongest open-source baseline by 8.0 points with a quarter of its time budget. Moreover, among six configurations spanning five heterogeneous agent pairs, HMA improves any-medal rate over the constituent baselines by 6.4 points on average, demonstrating cross-pair generality. A supplementary case on kernel optimization reaches 878 cycles, within 1.6% of the community leaderboard leader, demonstrating applicability beyond MLE.

items.title: Humans and Robots in Agriculture
items.abstract: Research in agricultural robotics has garnered increasing attention over the past decade. Simultaneously, Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) has emerged as a possible solution to increase automation and reduce the lack of human labor in the field. This chapter presents a study of research trends in HRI focusing on Artificial Intelligence (AI), human factors, and ergonomics in collaborative agricultural tasks. For example, we talk about the importance of robotics and the application of the different AI-based methods for HRI in field applications. Moreover, we emphasize situation awareness, stress, sleepiness, sleep quality, and distraction. We also explore various crucial and innovative topics related to HRI in agriculture, including safety, human factors, ergonomics, awareness, productivity, and management. This analysis shows that HRI paradigms can be effectively applied in agricultural applications, yielding promising production, safety, and farm management benefits, such as increasing productivity and reducing human workload.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Recruitment and Selection
items.abstract: Recruitment has always involved a mix of judgment and administration. Recruiters read applications, compare experience with job requirements, arrange interviews, and try to make a fair decision within a limited time. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools now assist with some of these tasks. They can sort resumes, match skills to vacancies, answer routine questions, and help schedule interviews. These uses may save time, but they also raise questions that cannot be answered by speed alone: are suitable candidates being identified, do applicants understand how they are assessed, and can the process disadvantage particular groups? This paper proposes a study of AI use in recruitment and selection, focusing on recruitment efficiency, perceived fairness, candidate experience, and the role of human review. A mixed-methods design is proposed. A questionnaire would gather responses from HR professionals, recruiters, job seekers, and employees, while interviews with a smaller group of HR professionals would provide more detailed examples. Academic publications and institutional reports would be used to frame the study. The paper does not present completed survey findings; its hypotheses and sample plan are proposals to be tested. The intended contribution is a practical, balanced account of how organizations can assess AI recruitment tools without assuming that automation is automatically faster, fairer, or more accurate

items.title: IMPACT OF MOTIVATION ON TEACHERS' JOB PERFORMANCE IN NIGER STATE, NIGERIA
items.abstract: This study investigated the impact of motivation on teachers' job performance in Niger State, Nigeria, using two dimensions of motivation, namely: intrinsic motivation and extrinsic motivation. Extrinsic motivation was conceptualized broadly in this study to capture both the material and structural incentives that an employer provides, such as salary, promotion, and recognition, and the physical and social conditions under which teaching and learning occur, such as classroom facilities, supervisory support, and school climate, consistent with the hygiene component of Herzberg's two factor theory. Intrinsic motivation on the other hand refers to motivation that originates internally in the form of a person's interests and goals. The study adopted a quantitative, cross sectional survey design. The total population of the study consisted of 6200 teachers obtained from the 25 Local Government Areas of Niger State distributed in the 3 senatorial districts of Niger-East, Niger-North and Niger-West. A multi stage sampling technique was adopted: the first stage involved stratifying the twenty-five local government areas by senatorial district, the second stage involved the random selection of a proportionate number of schools within each stratum, and the third stage involved the simple random selection of individual teacher respondents within the selected schools. The sample size was determined using the Taro Yamane formula, expressed as n = N / (1 + N(e)²), where n represents the required sample size, N represents the target population, and e represents the margin of error, set conventionally at 0.05 (Yamane, 1967). Applying this formula to the population of six thousand two hundred teachers yields a computed sample size of approximately three hundred and eighty (380) respondents. The instrument used for data collection produced a reliability index of 0.75. The research questions were answered using descriptive statistics, including mean, standard deviation and frequencies, alongside inferential statistics, specifically multiple regression analysis, to test the two null hypotheses at 0.05 level of confidence corresponding to the two motivational dimensions. The findings of the study indicated that both dimensions of motivation exert a positive and statistically significant impact on teachers' job performance, with extrinsic motivation, inclusive of the work environment, showing the strongest predictive weight. The study concludes that a deliberate, balanced motivational policy that addresses intrinsic fulfilment alongside extrinsic motivation-material incentives, the physical teaching environment; is necessary to sustain teachers’ job performance in Niger State. Recommendations are offered for the State Ministry of Education and the Universal Basic Education Board as well as School Managers/Administrators.

items.title: Implementing and Scaling Artificial Intelligence in Low-Resourced Radiation Oncology: A Systematic Review of Deployments
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to address workforce shortages and workflow inefficiencies in radiation oncology, particularly in low-resourced settings where limited specialist capacity constrains access to care. This systematic review evaluated AI deployments in radiation oncology in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and assessed readiness for safe implementation and scale-up. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, six databases were searched from January 2000 through December 2025. Eligible studies were classified using a radiation oncology-specific integration spectrum (Levels 0-4) and evaluated for workflow integration, validation, deployment, and governance characteristics. Eighteen studies met the inclusion criteria. Two studies (11.1%) focused on readiness or governance without clinical AI deployment (Level 0), nine (50.0%) reported task-level applications (Level 1), six (33.3%) demonstrated clinician-supervised workflow integration (Level 2), and one (5.6%) reported cross-stage workflow orchestration (Level 3). No study provided sufficient evidence for classification as Level 4 operation. Validation was predominantly retrospective, and continuous performance monitoring was not reported. AI deployment in LMIC radiation oncology remains concentrated at early stages of integration. This pattern reflects not a lack of innovation, but constraints in validation, workflow maturity, infrastructure, and governance. Safe and scalable deployment will require coordinated advances across these domains.

items.title: Information shock: how AI demands an evolution of information science
items.abstract: Purpose This paper argues that AI authoring is prompting an Information Shock and a new information science. The shock is not a matter of increased volume and variable quality of AI-produced information. It comes as generative AI creates a new kind of author that dissolves the document, the field’s organizing unit. This forces a reconstitution of tools, literacies and identity. Design/methodology/approach The paper applies a conceptual framework drawn from the history of Information Shocks, tracing how disruptions from cuneiform to post-World War II research data forced the field to rebuild around new objects and practices. AI is analyzed against that pattern. Findings AI produces two modes of authorship: document-like objects that enter existing infrastructures, and transactional, co-authored exchanges with no stable unit to catalog, retrieve, cite or verify. The second mode renders AI literacy inadequate, even in its current forms, because they presuppose an identifiable object and human interlocutors. Anticipated changes reach professional identity, tools, intellectual property and education. Research limitations/implications The argument is theoretical and prospective, and some anticipated changes remain speculative. The Information Shock outlined is anticipated to have major impacts for librarians and information professionals moving forward. Originality/value The paper offers a historically grounded distinction between document-producing and transactional AI authorship, arguing that AI is pushing the exchange to take the mediating position that the field has long held.

items.title: Informing users about LLMs' environmental costs encourages ethical consumption
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming deeply embedded in everyday human-AI interaction. However, the environmental costs associated with using those tools remain elusive. Here, we address the question of whether providing users with information about the environmental costs of using LLMs tempers their use. Such information highlights an ethical tension: acting pro-environmentally requires people to forgo some of the benefits AI tools provide. We study how people solve this trade-off in tasks that are relatively easy to tackle without using LLMs and further assess if the impact of providing such information has a stronger effect on people who have stronger environmental concerns. In two preregistered experiments (total N = 1,200), we studied participants’ use of ChatGPT in a text-editing task after they learned about the tool’s environmental costs. Results revealed that (i) raising awareness of ChatGPT’s environmental costs reduced its use and usage volume; (ii) interacting with a sycophantic model, one that encourages continuous use, did not attenuate the awareness effect, although it led to greater overall use; and (iii) raising awareness was especially effective among people with high environmental concerns. The findings highlight how raising awareness concerning LLM’s environmental costs can encourage responsible consumption.

items.title: Innovative Job Performance in Digitally Enabled Workplaces: A Systematic Review and Bibliometric Synthesis of Individual-Level Innovative Work Behavior
items.abstract: Innovative job performance (IJP) and innovative work behavior (IWB) are examined across distinct leadership, work-design, motivational, knowledge-sharing, and digital-work literatures. This review combines systematic full-text screening, bibliometric mapping, and a Theory–Context–Characteristics–Methodology (TCCM) synthesis to examine the individual-level evidence. The documented Scopus search of 19 September 2026 returned 23,225 records before database filters; 182 journal articles published in 2023–2026 were retained for Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny analysis. The available retrieval archive contained 90 PDF instances, including four exact duplicates. Of 86 unique full-text reports screened, 43 met the focused eligibility criteria. The 182-record bibliometric dataset covered 91 sources and 603 unique author names, with recurrent terms involving innovative work behavior, engagement, leadership, psychological empowerment, and knowledge sharing. The focused synthesis identified distinct organizational resources, motivational mechanisms, knowledge processes, and digital capabilities associated with IJP/IWB in the included studies. Much of the primary evidence relied on cross-sectional designs, and the higher-education substream was geographically concentrated. Within the bounded 182-record export, “excellencism” was absent from the searched metadata fields, and no record directly compared Generation Z and Millennials within an IJP/IWB model. The resulting conceptual framework should be interpreted as an evidence-informed synthesis rather than a causally validated model. Future research should improve temporal, multisource, multilevel, and measurement-invariant testing.

items.title: Instruction-Following LLM Agent for Simulating Human Memory Retrieval Process in Household Tasks
items.abstract: Human decision-making in dynamic household environments depends on memory retrieval processes that shape action selection and timing. This paper presents an instruction-following LLM agent as an executable human performance model for simulating memory retrieval behavior in household tasks. The proposed framework integrates memory encoding and decision-making modules with a modified ACT-R base-level activation equation that incorporates environmental entropy and observation duration. The framework was evaluated using human behavioral data from an AI2-THOR-based household task study. When predicting human search times, the modified equation produced lower prediction errors than the conventional ACT-R baseline, reducing MAE, RMSE, and MAPE by 11.08%, 5.37%, and 16.00%, respectively. These findings provide preliminary evidence that incorporating context-sensitive retrieval factors may support closer alignment with human search-time behavior in executable LLM-based human performance models.

items.title: Integrating generative artificial intelligence facilitates faculty interaction network and role transition in a biostatistics curriculum
items.abstract: In a two-year action-research study within an undergraduate biostatistics curriculum for nursing, pharmacy, and medical biotechnology students, we examined how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) facilitates educators to design, supervise, and evaluate learning. Students used GenAI first as a technical tutor and then as a partner in knowledge co-creation in case-based statistical problem-solving. Teachers’ reflection records and 4697 LINE messages during the study period were analyzed using qualitative coding, GenAI-assisted semantic analysis, and social network analysis. Teachers’ roles shifted from knowledge transmitters to facilitators of critical inquiry and human–GenAI co-learning. Overall, faculty communication was dense, reciprocal, and decentralized, whereas GenAI-related discourse was more selective and centralized. GenAI-related ties were less likely to form but, once formed, strongly reciprocal and locally clustered. GenAI integration can catalyze new forms of faculty leadership through expertise sharing and collaborative problem-solving. Intentional structures for cross-disciplinary exchange and reflective faculty development are needed.

items.title: Integrating technology anxiety into the TPB-TAM framework to examine AI adoption intention in hospital HRM: a study of Chinese healthcare professionals
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can empower healthcare professionals to make data-driven decisions and streamline administrative tasks in hospital human resource management (HRM). However, it is vital to understand their perceptions towards AI for seamless implementation in practice. Therefore, the study aimed to assess the role of technology anxiety within an integrated framework combining the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) to better understand adoption intentions in this high-stakes context. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 547 healthcare professionals working in hospitals across China. Data were analyzed using structural equation modeling, including confirmatory factor analysis, path analysis, and bootstrap mediation testing. Multi-group structural equation modeling was also used to compare healthcare professionals with different levels of AI familiarity. The integrated model explained 49.4% of the variance in behavioral intention, and all twelve hypothesized paths were statistically significant. Technology anxiety was negatively associated with perceived ease of use (β = -0.553, p < 0.001), perceived behavioral control (β = -0.371, p < 0.001), attitude (β = -0.339, p < 0.001), and subjective norms (β = -0.451, p < 0.001), and it was also associated with behavioral intention through multiple indirect pathways. Multi-group analysis showed that the association between perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness was stronger among professionals with low AI familiarity, while the remaining paths remained stable across groups. AI adoption intention in hospital HRM appears to involve more than rational evaluations of usefulness and ease of use. Emotional states, such as technology anxiety, also play a role. Reducing technology anxiety and improving ease of use for users with lower AI familiarity are therefore important steps for promoting AI adoption intention. These findings highlight the value of addressing emotional factors alongside cognitive beliefs when introducing AI tools in healthcare organizations.
